body: HTML's solution for this is the `datalist` element.

> HTML's solution for this is the datalist element.

It's unclear if datalist actually is the solution for this. This appears to be about filtering a bounded list of options (though I could be missing something?). datalist + input can be used for an unbounded combobox (where the input can contain a value not in the list of available options).

I think if this were to be done it would have to be a variant of option 2 (but the input would be inside of the picker instead of replacing the button), though simply allowing input in select via the parser is far from a complete solution the accessibility for this would need a lot of thought.

I would personally recommending raising an issue in OpenUI (or adding to an existing one), some thoughts on the unbounded combobox case can be found in https://open-ui.org/components/combobox.explainer/ (note its still early thoughts so the exact shape is very unlikely to match what we end up with).

i'd submit it's a bit of both.  For editable/type ahead comboboxes - `datalist` would work.

but then there are also UI where a select has LOTS of options, and custom components have been built to render an input (commonly as the first item in the popup) as a sibling to the custom select's options.

definitely agree this is a good topic to raise (re-raise really) over at open ui

These are all solid points. Thank you for helping move this discussion forward. I would contest that a datalist, while HTML's closest current solution, is rather a searchable list of suggestions that steer an input, which has some clear differences from a select element or a combobox for that matter.

Another option would be to implement a new attribute on the select element itself to enable this sort of filtering ability such as `filter` or `search`.
```html
<select filter="starts-with inclusive">
  <option>Apple</option>
  <option>Banana</option>
  <option>Cherry</option>
  <option>Date</option>
</select>
```

However, I think that would be redundant considering the inclusion of an input element, which can already be targeted with all the usual pseudo-classes relevant to it. Having the input element separate from the select element would also allow the input to exist outside of the select, somewhere else on the page. This is similar to how the Popover API works.

We can move this discussion to OpenUI but I'm curious why you don't consider input + datalist to be a combobox? What aspects of combobox doesn't it include? (If we for a second ignore the current rendering and stylability situation)
Here's at least one relevant openui issue fwiw: https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/847

I'm hoping the discussion also keeps a distinction between "combobox" as conceptually a text input with autocomplete to choose from versus a "filterable select", [shared an example](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/847#issuecomment-2270195223) that emphasizes the distinction:

For the set of options:
```html
  <optgroup label="Texas">
    <option>Paris</option>
  </optgroup>
  <optgroup label="France">
    <option>Paris</option>
  </optgroup>
```

Where a combobox's value on selection would be "Paris" and it would not be known which Paris is selected from the value while a filterable select would be a specific option that is distinguishable.

> We can move this discussion to OpenUI but I'm curious why you don't consider input + datalist to be a combobox? What aspects of combobox doesn't it include? (If we for a second ignore the current rendering and stylability situation)

I suppose the differences could boil down to styleability, so as long as that implementation could theoretically be designed to look exactly like a select element, with the dropdown itself being the input or search, and the datalist options not being limited (and being able to scroll naturally), I guess that would be similar enough.

Reusing that could work, but I think it could still be improved by being styled to look and function like most standard combo boxes and by offering different filtering techniques.

> I'm hoping the discussion also keeps a distinction between "combobox" as conceptually a text input with autocomplete to choose from versus a "filterable select", [shared an example](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/847#issuecomment-2270195223) that emphasizes the distinction: …

Yes, this was my thought as well.

One other significantly important difference here is that a filterable select—much like many of the combobox implementations we see today—should support multi-select. In fact, it should have all the same affordances that a `select` element naturally has.

Thanks for filing this! I agree this is a use case that is worth implementing.

I think that there are two variations of this: one has the text input in the page, and the other has the text input in the popup. It looks like this proposal is focused on putting the text input in the page, and I'm kind of hoping that variation can be handled by improving `<input>` with `<datalist>`. I also acknowledge that use case seems more prevalent, such as in google.com.

I also think that if you want to force the user to choose from of a set of predefined options instead of letting the user enter anything as their value, then the `<select>` element with some sort of filtering mechanism is better than `<input>` with `<datalist>`.

Here are some examples I'm aware of on the web which put the text filter inside the popup:
- https://select2.org/getting-started/basic-usage#single-select-boxes
- dom.forms.selectSearch in firefox's about:config ([screenshot](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/847#issuecomment-1738617411))
- https://www.temu.com/bgp_region_setting.html

Thanks @josepharhar. I appreciate the feedback. I think the location of the input is more of a design detail. I agree we could improve the `<input>`/`<datalist>` pattern, but at the end of the day, it's still an input that accepts an arbitrary string, unlike the case I'm accounting for here where the field itself can only be filled with one of the `<select>` element's option values.

The example you shared at https://select2.org/getting-started/basic-usage#single-select-boxes are exactly the kind of functionality I am advocating for with this proposal, but with the flexibility of having that input (1) exist inside the `<select>` options as is seen at that link, (2) double as the form control, (3) or even exist outside the `<select>` element entirely.

`<datalist>` appears to operate more as a set of hints, and even if validation options were added to invalidate the field if a value other than one of the `datalist` values is used, it would not be able to block the use of such values entirely without supplementing with JS.

Actually, the example titled "Multi-select boxes" on that same page is one of the cases I specifically seek to solve for here. One key difference here too is that the `id` of the selected value(s) is what is passed with a ``/`` pattern, which also appears to always show the `value` and `textContent` of its options: ![](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e09a37fa-336e-4b06-97cd-7d314073f320)

This proposal seems to couple many different things and tries to solve many different problems at once. Let's try to disentagle them.

## Combobox vs autocomplete

A combobox is fundamentally different from a searachable select, even though both are dropdowns with a searchable list of options. One constrains the user choice within the available options and the other aids the user by suggesting common inputs, but does not constrain them in any way. A `<datalist>` + `<input>` affords the combobox pattern, not the searchable select pattern.

Additionally, `<datalist>` as currently implemented is imperfect for combobox patterns, because it provides no way to make the internal value invisible, in the way a `<select>` does. There is no way to follow the `<select>` pattern of having separate user-friendly labels and separate machine-readable values. You _can_ have options with separate values and labels, but when selected, the `value` is entered in the input, not the label. Since inputs do not support separate labels and values, it's unclear how else that could possibly work. Having a separate presentational value and a separate submitted value could be useful functionality in general, e.g. for date formatting, number formatting and so on, so perhaps there is a separate proposal there.

## Customizing how the filtering works

Customizing how the filtering happens is something that is not only useful here, but also for `<datalist>` and it seems should be solved together for both, but I see it as separate from adding filtering functionality to selects. Just like `<datalist>` shipped with UA-defined filtering, so can this.

For `<datalist>` one question is whether that is behavior that should be specified on the `<datalist>` itself, or the `<input>`, which can only be answered via use cases. Usually they are 1-1 so this doesn't matter, but often they are not. I can't think of use cases where it needs to be different for the same set of data, so I'm leaning towards making it part of the `<datalist>`, but more research is needed.

Additionally, whatever declarative solution we come up for making common cases easy, ideally there should also be a JS API for  making complex cases possible (fuzzy search, AI search, remote loaded options etc). Otherwise, authors will still resort to reimplementing these controls.

## Ease of use vs power curve

Authors should not have to code filtering by themselves just to style the filtering input. If they don't care about styling the filtering input or customizing its behavior, they should not need to provide one. I can't remember what was decided about native elements using slots, but IMO it's a great mechanism for this type of progressive customization with sensible defaults.

From a UX point of view, **any select with more than a certain number of options _should_ be searchable**. There is certainly a gray area, but I have trouble thinking of use cases where searchability is not desirable in a select with several dozen options (such as a country selector). Most OSes afford some basic searchability through typing, but this is an undiscoverable power user feature, since the typed characters are not visible.

So, I would even argue that at least for unstyled selects in the dropdown state with more than N options, the filtering should be there **by default**. 

## Putting it together

I'd propose:
- An attribute to enable/disable filtering, with the default being `auto`, which enables filtering when in the dropdown state and there are more than N options (which could even be UA-dependent). 
	- The attribute can be later expanded with values to declaratively customize how the filtering works.
	- Potential names: `filterable`, `searachable`
	- A way to define a function to customize how the filtering works (not MVP). 
		- Perhaps `HTMLOptionElement.matchesFilter(text)` (though then it would need to be set on every `<option>` and these are often dynamically added/removed)
		- Alternatively, `HTMLSelectElement.matchesFilter(text, option)` (with a corresponding `HTMLDataListElement` attribute)
- By default, the filter is a shadow DOM `<input>` which can be accessed through a pseudo-element (e.g. `::select-filter`). For more customizability, authors can slot in their own `<input>`.

Thanks Lea! I also shared some thoughts on how the text input could be exposed/controlled here, and I think there is a lot of overlap between our ideas: https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/847#issuecomment-2876984892

I like the filterable/searchable attribute with different values, as that could address the need to change how filtering works:
- https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/847#issuecomment-2877017007
- https://open-ui.org/components/combobox.explainer/#introducing-search-attribute

The matchesFilter method is interesting. If we expose a more generic way for the author to control filtering by reacting to changes to the text filter input, I'm not sure it would be necessary?

> By default, the filter is a shadow DOM `<input>` which can be accessed through a pseudo-element (e.g. `::select-filter`). For more customizability, authors can slot in their own `<input>`.

Allowing authors to slot their own `<input>` would be great so that authors can truly react to changes and dynamically add options (Luke pointed this out [here](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/847#issuecomment-2877017007)).
However, how does that work with the filterable/searchable attribute? If the author provides an `<input>` but doesn't set the attribute, what should it do? Maybe this could be a "manual" mode where the user can type into the text input but no filtering happens automatically, and the author could react to changes there and implement their own filtering.
In order to support this, we would also have to make additional HTML parser changes to allow `<input>` in `<select>`, which I'm not sure would be web compatible. If we are slotting the `<input>` into a special slot, then we would need to allow `<input>` as a direct child of `<select>`, which will break some sites.
